articles.content:
Labor Day weekend is over, and summer is in the rearview mirror for another year. You know what that means: school. And as you rush your kids out the door to the bus or carpool, it’s likely with a bowl of cereal in their bellies.
My mom didn’t let us have “sugar cereals,” as she called them, so whenever I got the chance (at a friend’s house, usually), I’d devour Peanut Butter Cap’n Crunch like I’d been starving in the desert for weeks. Then it was back to Cheerios—though I’ve moved on to cereals with even less sugar these days. Getting old is fun!
As cereal season gets underway for another year, we thought it would be fun to take a look at which cereals are the most popular around the country. And lucky for us, CSP Global, which offers accredited nursing programs in St. Paul, Minnesota, and Portland, Oregon, had already done the heavy lifting.
Ahead, I’ll take you state by state through their delicious survey results filled with cereals you remember as a kid and eat now as an adult. Read on to get a bowlful of knowledge about this breakfast favorite.

We do a lot of Googling these days, so instead of mining grocery stores for sales data or calling people on their phones (who answers those calls, anyway?), CSP Global analyzed Google Trends data to find out exactly which cereals Americans were hungry for.
Why did they do this, you might ask? Because they’re a nursing school, CSP Global wanted to get a sense of state and regional trends to start a conversation about nutrition and health. Cereal aisles across the country look pretty much the same, but when you really drill down on what people are searching for, some definite trends emerge.
When you take a look at this list, it’s apparent there’s not a lot of turnover in the cereal world. These are the same old classics we’ve been eating for decades. My mother would definitely not approve of most of them, but they sure sound delicious to me right about now.
Here are the most popular cereals in each state:
Froot Loops took the cereal crown with wins in 13 states and was by far the most searched cereal in the entire country. And it wasn’t even close: The tropical-fruit-flavored sugar bomb’s closest competition, Cheerios (yes!) and Rice Krispies, each won only 5 states apiece.
The cereal analysts also broke out the searches regionally, and it looks like the South gave Froot Loops its dominating win. The Northeast and the Midwest (my old stomping ground) went for the basic grains. Out in the sunny West, Honey Bunches of Oats came in first.
My beloved old home state of Minnesota was the only state to pick Wheaties … which actually isn’t too much of a surprise, now that I think of it. A Minneapolis radio station aired the very first cereal jingle in 1926, and it was for, yep, Wheaties.
What is surprising is that wheat, in general, turns out to be an unpopular cereal grain, at least as far as searches go. Raisin Bran won only one state, Maine, and Frosted Mini-Wheats also came out on top in a single state, Wyoming.
Here’s another head-scratcher: When is the last time you ate Apple Jacks? I didn’t even know it was still around, but Mississippi loves it. Finally, my old neighbor Iowa is the only state pulling for Cap’n Crunch (but not the clearly superior Peanut Butter version). Funny, I would have thought they’d be all-in for Corn Pops.

articles.title: Here’s Why We Still Have Dreams About Being in School—And What Each Type of Weird School Dream Means
articles.content:
It’s been 35 years since I was in high school. And yet, multiple nights a year, I find myself roaming those halls once again. The details shift slightly each time, but the gist is always the same: I walk into school only to discover that I have a final exam coming up in English (sometimes it’s history)—a class I had no idea I was enrolled in and therefore haven’t shown up to once the entire year. How am I going to pull this off? Will the teacher realize she hasn’t seen me all year and fail me automatically? I don’t even know where the classroom is! The panic is so overwhelmingly real, and I start reprimanding myself for having been so irresponsible and for putting myself in what feels like an impossible situation. And then, just like that, I wake up. I’m so relieved … but also so rattled. Granted, I wasn’t the best student, and I cut my fair share of classes back in the day, but I was never that clueless. Why does my subconscious do that to me, not to mention bring me back to that time in my life at all? I’m so far past that stage—I have kids who have since graduated from high school! What’s really terrifying? So many of us have that same exact dream. A recent Amerisleep survey of more than 2,000 people found that being back in school is among the most common recurring dreams out there, right up there with falling and being chased. And in a Psychology Today blog post that surveyed people describing their own recurring school dreams, the most common version reported was almost identical to mine: discovering you’d been enrolled in a class all along, never once attending, and then scrambling to find the exam room on the day it finally counts. We asked three dream experts—two psychotherapists and a professional dream analyst—to help decode why so many of us are still, apparently, failing a class we may have finished decades ago. Read on to find out what’s going on, what some of our most common school dreams mean and whether they actually have anything to do with school at all. Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more psychology, life tips, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long. Think of your brain as a warehouse, says Katie Rose, a Manhattan-based psychotherapist. Every day, “boxes” of new experiences get dropped off in a staging area, and your brain’s internal workers—networks involving the hippocampus and amygdala, which handle memory and emotion—sort through them and file them away across a web of connected brain regions. When you dream, your brain pulls old boxes back off the shelf. And as levels of neurotransmitters shift during REM sleep—acetylcholine rises, stimulating cortical activity and prompting vivid imagery, while norepinephrine and serotonin drop to unusually low levels—those boxes don’t always get put back together the way they were. “The connections your brain makes can be more emotional, symbolic and sometimes seemingly nonsensical than they would be when you’re awake,” Rose says. “During REM, the brain is far from inactive,” notes John Mayer, PhD, a clinical psychologist based in Chicago. Visual-association areas generate the imagery you see, even though your eyes aren’t taking in any actual visual information, while the amygdala and related limbic structures—which process emotion, threat and personal significance—stay highly active. That’s part of why dreams can feel so emotionally intense. Memory plays a role too. The hippocampus, which organizes autobiographical and episodic memories, supplies fragments of both recent and older experiences. But rather than replaying a memory exactly as it happened, “the dreaming brain recombines people, places and emotions into new images and stories,” Mayer says. Meanwhile, the brain’s usual reality-check system—the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, responsible for logic and working memory—is comparatively quiet. That may be why dreams entail bizarre events. Overall, Mayer explains, “the visual brain is creating, the emotional brain is reacting, the memory system is supplying material, and the logical brain is operating with reduced supervision.”
So why does school, specifically, keep getting pulled off the shelf—even for people decades removed from their last final exam? According to our experts, there are a few explanations. “We spent thousands of hours of our formative years in school—it was the primary space for our learning and social lives,” Rose says. “We would have experienced intensely vulnerable situations there, likely for the first time.” Think: embarrassment over struggling with a new subject, rejection from a friend group or a first taste of real success and leadership. “It makes sense that our brains return to that place in adulthood,” she says. “If our brains are trying to work out a feeling, it may return to school to try to understand the origin of that feeling.”
“School is often a go-to for stress because the certainty that one would have stressful experiences in school is extremely high,” Mayer says. “This is the first time a child will have these pressures outside of the home when they first attend school—that’s significant and embedded in our brain.” And those stressful experiences only build over the years, from first grade through graduation. “School was the original training ground for job stress,” says Lauri Loewenberg, a professional dream analyst and the author of Dream on It. “It’s where we first learned the pressure of deadlines, preparation, performance, evaluation, competition, fitting in and moving up to the next level.” Because those emotional associations were formed there, she explains, “school remains the face your subconscious often gives to career stress, even decades after you’ve graduated.”
“I think of it less as the brain saying, ‘A math test means work stress,’ and more as the brain looking for the closest emotional match it has available,” Rose says. In other words, “the math test may not be about math at all,” she says. “It may be the box your brain has on the shelf for ‘This is what it feels like when I am being evaluated and I’m not sure I’m going to be good enough.'”
“Less often, finding yourself back in school or a class setting in your dream can mean you are currently learning something new in your life—such as a new skill, a new mindset or behavior, a life lesson or basically any situation where you would consider yourself to be ‘learning the ropes,'” Loewenberg says. So if you’re navigating a career pivot, learning how to play mahjong or getting up to speed on new software at work, that classroom feeling may just be your brain reaching for the closest thing it has on file for “still figuring this out.”
These dreams don’t strike at random. “Dreams are always triggered by some stimulus in our perceptional system,” Mayer notes. Back-to-school season is a classic trigger—store ads, kids heading back to class or just the general rhythm of the calendar can all seep into your dreams, whether or not you’re conscious of it. Not all school dreams are created equal, and some are definitely more stressful than others. Here’s what our experts say about some of the most common variations. This is likely the most common school dream. Mayer hears a version of this constantly in his practice—patients dreaming they have a test to take and are completely unprepared, or that they never actually finished their degree and are secretly an imposter. Loewenberg adds: “This dream is often connected to feeling unprepared for an upcoming situation that feels like a big deal. It could be anything from a board meeting or job interview to something more personal, like meeting your future in-laws for the first time.”
She suggests asking yourself: What situation in my waking life feels similar right now? Where do I feel like I’m going to be scrutinized? Where do I really have to prove myself, but I’m feeling uncertain, insecure or not quite up to the task? The fix isn’t to obsess over being perfectly prepared, she says—it’s to get specific about what would actually help. “Your dream may be highlighting an area where your confidence needs to catch up with your expectations.”
This one, according to Loewenberg, is less about the test itself and more about the search. “This dream is often the result of feeling that you aren’t where you should be in some area of your waking life,” she says. “It’s a common dream when you haven’t found a job or career that feels like home to you, or when you aren’t quite where you feel you should be in your career.”
The searching itself is the important part. “You’re looking for the classroom because, symbolically, you’re looking for where you belong, where you’re supposed to be focusing your energy or what your next step should be,” Loewenberg explains. Her suggested reframe: Instead of asking why you’re not where you should be, ask why you actually want to be. According to Loewenberg, exes rarely show up in dreams to represent themselves. “The high school sweetheart is often our first experience of romantic love,” she says. “So when they show up in a dream, they usually aren’t playing themselves. Rather, they’re standing in for the feelings we first experienced with them: excitement, desire, butterflies, infatuation, feeling chosen or that feeling of never wanting to be apart.”
The trick to decoding it, she says, is to ask what first comes to mind when you think of that person and why that particular feeling might be relevant right now. “If the relationship was wonderful, perhaps you’re craving that kind of excitement, attention, freedom or romance again,” she says. But if the relationship was a bad one, don’t assume the dream is a sign you want them back. Loewenberg suggests asking yourself: Is anything happening in my life now that makes me feel the way I felt with that person? The bottom line: Focus on the feeling, not the person. According to Loewenberg, nothing in a dream is truly random—especially the cast of characters. Dreams borrow from the past in order to give us a message that will help us in our present. “Everything and everyone in your dream stands in for some part of you or for something that is directly affecting you,” she says, “unless it is someone you deal with on a daily basis, like your spouse or your child.”
So, she explains, the way to figure out why you’re dreaming of Josh from chemistry class is to ask yourself what first comes to mind when you think of him. If you remember Josh being the class clown, then that’s what is at play. “It’s not about Josh,” Loewenberg says. It’s about what’s relevant to you currently: not taking things too seriously and having a sense of humor right now. Loewenberg says most dreams that put you back in a classroom actually keep you as your current-day self—the classroom is just a familiar backdrop your brain reaches for. “The school setting becomes a metaphor for something you’re currently learning, struggling with, being tested on or feeling unprepared for,” she says. So if you dream you’re back in a lecture hall, quizzes and all, but you’re still very much you—crow’s feet, mortgage, hot flashes—it’s probably not about school at all. It’s about whatever test you feel like you’re taking in real life right now, whether that’s a big presentation, a medical diagnosis or just proving to yourself you can still hack it. According to the Psychology Today survey of people describing their recurring school dreams, 73% of respondents set their dream in high school, compared with 34% in college, 12% in elementary school and 7% in middle school or junior high. Loewenberg says the specific setting is meaningful, not incidental: “The different stages of school can reflect different stages of learning, growth, confidence or challenge in your waking life.”
Rose adds that the setting tends to be personal rather than universal. “Typically, the school where you experienced the most prominent social-emotional growth will be where your brain returns to,” she says.

“这将因个人经历而异。”确实，大脑反复重播而非释放的原因是有科学依据的。梅耶尔（Mayer）将大脑比作“一台庞大的主机计算机”，它会“循环反复处理这些数据”，直到情况发生改变。罗斯（Rose）对这种重复的看法则较少依赖字面意义。她表示：“我认为梦境并没有特定的含义，但它们是大脑赋予我们世界意义的方式。”在她看来，重复出现的梦境并非一个带有隐藏答案的谜题，而是大脑在反复处理未解决的情感，直到这种情感的处理方式发生变化。

好消息是：每次梦到考试或初中同桌时，不必彻底改变生活。但如果学校梦境持续出现，专家一致认为值得关注——以下各种技巧提供了不同的角度来理解。

在读者文摘，我们致力于由熟悉领域且具经验的作家创作高质量内容，并与相关合格专家合作。我们依赖可靠的初级来源，包括政府和专业组织、学术机构，以及适当情况下的作家个人经历。我们核实所有事实和数据，以可信来源为依据，并定期更新以确保内容的准确性和时效性。了解更多关于我们的团队、贡献者和编辑政策。

But if the relationship was a bad one, don’t assume the dream is a sign you want them back. Loewenberg suggests asking yourself: Is anything happening in my life now that makes me feel the way I felt with that person? The bottom line: Focus on the feeling, not the person.

You’re with random classmates you haven’t thought about in years

According to Loewenberg, nothing in a dream is truly random—especially the cast of characters. Dreams borrow from the past in order to give us a message that will help us in our present. “Everything and everyone in your dream stands in for some part of you or for something that is directly affecting you,” she says, “unless it is someone you deal with on a daily basis, like your spouse or your child.”

So, she explains, the way to figure out why you’re dreaming of Josh from chemistry class is to ask yourself what first comes to mind when you think of him. If you remember Josh being the class clown, then that’s what is at play. “It’s not about Josh,” Loewenberg says. It’s about what’s relevant to you currently: not taking things too seriously and having a sense of humor right now.

You’re going back to school as an adult

Loewenberg says most dreams that put you back in a classroom actually keep you as your current-day self—the classroom is just a familiar backdrop your brain reaches for. “The school setting becomes a metaphor for something you’re currently learning, struggling with, being tested on or feeling unprepared for,” she says. So if you dream you’re back in a lecture hall, quizzes and all, but you’re still very much you—crow’s feet, mortgage, hot flashes—it’s probably not about school at all. It’s about whatever test you feel like you’re taking in real life right now, whether that’s a big presentation, a medical diagnosis or just proving to yourself you can still hack it.

Does the meaning change if your dream is about elementary school, high school or college?

According to the Psychology Today survey of people describing their recurring school dreams, 73% of respondents set their dream in high school, compared with 34% in college, 12% in elementary school and 7% in middle school or junior high.

Loewenberg says the specific setting is meaningful, not incidental: “The different stages of school can reflect different stages of learning, growth, confidence or challenge in your waking life.”

  • Elementary school “often points to something that is in its early or introductory stages,” Loewenberg says. You may be just starting out or dealing with something that feels simple and manageable. But personal history matters too: If you were bullied in those years, dreaming of elementary school “could indicate that something or someone in your current life is making you feel vulnerable, picked on, excluded or powerless in a similar way.”
  • High school “tends to take things up a notch,” Loewenberg says, since it’s typically associated with “social pressures, identity, popularity, fitting in, first relationships, competition, independence and figuring out who you are.” A high school dream might reflect feeling judged, compared or pressured to perform in your current life.
  • College, she says, “can represent a more advanced level of learning and development.” It might show up when you’re tackling something more complex, taking on more responsibility or being pushed to grow beyond what you already know.

Rose adds that the setting tends to be personal rather than universal. “Typically, the school where you experienced the most prominent social-emotional growth will be where your brain returns to,” she says. “That will be highly individual based on your experiences.”

Why do certain school dreams recur?

Yes, there’s a reason your brain keeps replaying it instead of letting it go. Mayer compares the brain to “a huge mainframe computer” that will “cycle and cycle that data over and over again” until something changes.

Rose takes a less literal view of what the repetition is doing. “I don’t think our dreams mean anything,” she says, “but they are our brain’s way of making meaning of our world.” A dream on a loop, in her view, isn’t a puzzle with a hidden answer—it’s the brain circling back to an unresolved feeling until something changes how that feeling gets processed.

What should you do when you have one of these dreams?

The good news: You don’t need to overhaul your life every time you dream about a pop quiz or the kid who sat next to you in homeroom. But if a school dream keeps showing up, our experts agree it’s worth paying attention—and each technique below offers a different way in.

  • Give the dream a new ending. In his clinical work, Mayer uses a technique he calls “finish off your dream.” If a recurring dream is bothering you, rewrite the ending in a powerful, positive way—for example, turning a failed-test dream into one where you ace the exam and the teacher praises you in front of the class, or picturing your diploma on the wall if the dream involves never having graduated. “Make your finish big, fantastic and positive,” he says. Giving the dream a deliberate, positive ending “puts closure on the dreams” and can stop the loop.
  • Talk it through out loud. Rose adds that you shouldn’t assume there’s some hidden message that needs to be decoded—it’s more useful to get curious about what the dream brings up emotionally. “Talking it through out loud with a friend or therapist can be even more helpful” than journaling alone, she says, since putting an internal experience into words can break the cycle of rumination. In sessions, she asks patients what parts of the dream stand out most to them, then works with them to connect it to themes in their present life—or simply to retell the old story “through an awake, adult lens.” As she puts it, “the act of processing the dream out loud is the work.”
  • Work from the feeling, not the plot. Loewenberg suggests asking yourself what’s happening in your current life that matches the dream’s emotional tone—unprepared, searching for direction, nostalgic, judged, in over your head—and letting that be your real clue, rather than fixating on the literal details of the dream itself.
  • Know when to bring in outside help. Mayer says that if these dreams are affecting your daily functioning or adding real stress to your day, it may be time to talk to a therapist rather than just riding it out.

About the experts

  • Katie Rose, LCSW, is a Manhattan-based psychotherapist with more than a decade of experience working with individuals and couples.
  • John Mayer, PhD, is a clinical psychologist, the author of Family Fit: Find Your Balance in Life and the creator of the podcast Anxiety’s a B!tch. He is recognized for his intervention and clinical work on sleep and dreaming, and also holds seminars for other professionals on helping patients get better sleep.
  • Lauri Loewenberg is a professional dream analyst, the author of Dream on It and the creator of the dream-interpretation app Dream Chat with Lauri.

Why trust us

那晚在睡前滚动Instagram时，我永远不会忘记那种被打击的感觉（尽管我是健康作家，也不总是有最健康的习惯）——看到整个闺蜜群聚在一起为生日宴会干杯的照片。所有人都在照片中……除了我。这让我这种成年女性当场哭出声来，声响之大还让丈夫从隔壁冲了进来。我一边哭一边疯狂回溯短信，看看是否错过邀请。我是否不小心静音了群聊？邮件是否被分到了垃圾箱？是否有黑客或外星人参与？

原来，我只是没被邀请。

第二天见到其中一位女生，我小心翼翼地问晚会如何。她镇定地看了我一眼，叹了口气："我知道这会伤你的心，但你得放下。不是每个人都能被邀请参加每件事。"

这番话让我喘不过气来。（这就是我得知自己被踢出朋友圈的方式。）

不过，我也有过另一种经历。在策划活动时，我意识到邀请所有好友是不切实际的，除非我想租用会议中心、聘请宴会服务员并获得酒类许可证。有时候，你只能选择。你知道比没被邀请更糟糕的事是什么吗？就是盯着邀请名单想：天啊，谁会被淘汰？

尽管我的"朋友"（前朋友？）的态度不太友善，但她说得对。不是每个人都能被邀请参加每件事。当然，并非每次漏邀都意味着你被踢出群体，也并非每份精心筛选的邀请名单都会让你感到自己是怪物。但细节才是关键。

所以，真的很没礼貌若不邀请整个朋友圈参加夜晚聚会吗？如何在不陷入决策瘫痪或租用活动大厅的情况下处理这种情况？又如何应对难免发生的伤心情绪——尤其是当它们是你自己的时？让我们来看看。

归根结底，这是个实用性问题。某些场所和活动根本无法容纳整个朋友圈。餐厅有桌子限制。音乐会有票数限制。某人的客厅在放下拼盘后大约只剩3平方英尺的空间。而婚礼邀请名单可以严峻到让原本理性的成年人考虑移居他国。

但关键是：成年人拥有分层的关系完全正常。根据邓巴的社交理论，大多数人只能维持约150个有意义的关系（称为邓巴数），这些关系自然形成多层圈子。最内层大约是5个人：你的生死之交，即使凌晨2点遇到紧急情况也会立即联系的人。中间圈大约15人，是你经常见的朋友。接下来50人是你的烧烤和生日派对伙伴。最大的圈子包含约150个可以保持相当亲密联系的人。拥有这样的友情亚群并非对整个群体的背叛，这只是友情的运作方式。

友谊不是一个巨大的桶，标签为"我必须永远邀请的人"。有时你想举办盛大的生日派对。其他时候，你可能想和三个最好的朋友吃墨西哥卷饼，花两个小时讨论你刚花在护肤霜上的令人震惊的金额。这没问题。而且，保持聚会规模小也有很多其他理由。也许活动只适合部分朋友。也许两个人不合，你不想在啖着马蒂尼酒的同时处理冲突。也许你想与一两个人深入讨论某个私人话题。也许你只是六个月没见某个朋友了，想要独处时间。

友谊可以有亚群。实际上，如果你们认识超过五分钟，它们几乎肯定存在。然而，说"我现在需要更小的群体"与"我想让所有人知道没被选中"之间存在巨大差异。

受伤的心。困难之处在于，对一个人来说完全合理的邀请决定，对另一个人来说可能感觉像是社会性麻风病宣告。处于第二或第三圈的人可能相信自己属于内心圈——然后在吃着Cap'n Crunch糖果早餐时打开Instagram时发现事实并非如此。我知道这一点，因为……请参阅上述。

研究表明，社会排斥会以非常真实的方式伤害人。巴塞尔大学和普渡大学的研究人员研究了人们日常生活中陌生感的影响，发现这些被忽视或排斥的平凡经历会动摇人们对安全、幸福和归属感的基本感受。最近，巴塞尔大学和科布伦茨-兰茨大学的研究人员特别研究了社交媒体排斥。在涉及1,149名参与者的五项研究中，他们发现仅仅在Instagram上未被@到某个帖子可能会损害人们的心理健康，尤其是那些归属感需求强烈的人。被排除在照片之外更令人沮丧。

没错，我们的大脑似乎可以看到六个女人吃着玉米片的照片时，反应像是文明本身拒绝了我们。这对于一盘奶酪薯片来说是非常高的情感代价。有时这种信息是无意的，但有时不是。邀请是行使群体内权力、控制或地位的一种方式。即使排斥并非刻意残忍，信息仍可能传达：我选择了他们。我没选你。

尽管如此，这并不意味着你应该邀请所有人参加所有活动。这意味着如果你在做选择，你应该了解风险，并认识到这可能对友谊产生影响。

我不确定我是否曾经处理过如此多灰色地带的礼仪问题。整个答案本身就是一个穿着风衣的巨大灰色地带。在决定你的来宾名单是否完全合理，或者你是否将成为某人故事中的反派之前，我会问以下问题。

有多少人被排除在外？如果你有一个10人的群体，而你邀请了9人参加周五晚上的活动，那么你并没有创造一个亲密环境——你创造了一个冷漠女孩群体。

这种情况有多常发生？如果只是此次且有充分理由，可能问题不大。但如果同一个人始终神秘般不被邀请——生日派对、墨西哥卷饼星期二、满月下裸舞——那么你需要考虑他们是否真的是朋友。

原始群体有多大？如果你正在协调15个朋友的女孩夜晚，那么再多一个人又如何？另一方面，如果你计划四人晚餐，那么增加一两个人确实会造成显著变化。

这真的是一个群体吗？如果这些人属于一个明确定义的朋友群，经常一起活动，排除一两个人会感觉更尖锐。但如果你邀请的是几个偶然认识的互相认识的朋友，可能没有期望每次社交活动都包括所有人。

这个计划如何演变？"两个人已经约好见面，再加入两个人"与"我列出20人名单，然后选择我最喜欢的五个人"之间存在差异。前者感觉自然。后者感觉像是《单身汉》，只是没有玫瑰，所有人都有截图。

夜晚聚会在哪里？如果你去私人场所或进行自然限制群体规模的活动，可以灵活安排。但如果你去公共场所，可能会遇到共同朋友甚至可能遇到未被邀请的朋友，至少应该考虑他们的感受。

这个活动有多正式？提前两周安排并发送日历邀请的正式女孩夜晚与自发去In-N-Out有完全不同的感觉。自发性赋予你一些礼仪上的宽容。

是否邀请孩子或伴侣？有时朋友圈只是女孩们之间，有时则是家庭或情侣聚会。只需确保每个人都清楚这一点。

最重要的是：被邀请的人如何得知自己未被邀请？理想情况下，他们不会知道。现实中，他们很可能会知道。如果你的朋友不得不通过Instagram故事、标记的Facebook照片或健身房的谈话得知你的晚餐，这可能会让一个本应合理的决定变得更痛苦。

我的朋友的"让它过去吧"态度粗鲁，但至少她诚实。太多人试图隐藏或减轻这种情况，认为这样可以照顾他人的感受。但一旦有人发现八个朋友一起出去而没有邀请他们，他们的感受已经受伤。假装相反并不能消除痛苦。这只是增加了第二层尴尬。

你不需要为和其他人吃饭道歉。但你需要承认你的朋友可能感到难过。简单的一句"我能理解为什么这让你难过。这并非想表达我对你的感受"可以起到很大作用。注意，我并没有说"抱歉没带你一起吃饭"。你可以有其他朋友。你可以和不同的人有不同的友谊。你可以偶尔不用先组建一个30人的委员会就和某人度过一个晚上。

如果你想保持一个体面的人，你不能做的是，当某人发现其他人一起出去而没有邀请他们时，感到被排除在外却装作困惑。情感并不总是符合逻辑。不幸的是，它们也是不可避免的。

不邀请某人参加聚会并非没礼貌。但有时不邀请某人参加聚会可能是没礼貌的。我知道这是一个极不满意的答案。欢迎来到礼仪世界。
articles.summary:
I’ll never forget the gut punch of scrolling through Instagram one night before bed (just because I’m a health writer doesn’t mean I always have the healthiest habits) and seeing it: a picture of my entire group of close girl friends out to dinner, toasting to celebrate a birthday. Everyone was in the picture … except me. It was such a shock that I, a woman well into adulthood, burst into tears so loud that my husband came running in from the next room. As I wept, I frantically scrolled back through texts to see if I’d somehow missed an invite. Did I mute the group text by accident? Did my email send it to spam? Were hackers or aliens involved? 

Nope. I just wasn’t invited. 

The next day, when I saw one of the women, I gingerly asked how the party was. She looked at me sharply and sighed, “I knew that was going to hurt your feelings, but you need to get over it. Not everyone can be invited to everything.” 

That hurt so much it took my breath away. (That was also how I learned I’d been ejected from the friend group.)

That said, I’ve been on the other side too. I’ve planned events and realized that inviting all of my close friends is not logistically feasible unless I want to rent a convention center, hire a catering staff and obtain a liquor license. Sometimes you simply have to choose. And you know what’s sometimes worse than being the person who gets left off the guest list? Being the person staring at the guest list thinking, Well, crap. Who gets cut?

As unkind as my friend (ex-friend?) was, she wasn’t wrong. Not everyone can be invited to everything. It’s not always that dramatic, of course. Not every missed invite means you’re booted from the group, and not every curated invitation list will make you feel like a monster. But the devil is in the details.

So is it really rude not to invite your entire friend group to a night out? How do you navigate that situation without being paralyzed by indecision or renting an event hall? And how do you deal with the hurt feelings that will inevitably happen—especially when they are yours? Let’s figure it out below.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

The case for not inviting everyone

It boils down to practicality. Some venues and activities simply can’t accommodate an entire friendship ecosystem. Restaurants have tables. Concerts have tickets. Someone’s living room has approximately 3 square feet of available floor space once you put down the charcuterie board. And wedding invite lists can be so intense, they can cause otherwise rational adults to consider moving to another country.

But here’s the thing: It’s completely normal for adults to have relationship tiers. According Dunbar’s Social Theory, most of us can sustain only about 150 meaningful relationships (called Dunbar’s number), with those relationships naturally forming in nested circles. The innermost circle is roughly five people: your ride-or-dies, who you’d call at 2 a.m. in an emergency. The middle circle contains about 15 folks, and they’re the friends you see regularly. The next circle, about 50 friends, are your barbecue-and-birthday-party people. And the largest circle contains approximately 150 people you can maintain reasonably close connections with. Having these types of subgroups of friends isn’t a betrayal of the larger group; it’s just how friendship works. 

Friendship is not one giant bucket labeled PEOPLE I AM OBLIGATED TO INVITE FOREVER. Sometimes you want to have a huge birthday bash. Other times, you want to have tacos with your three best friends and spend two hours discussing the alarming amount of money you just spent on a moisturizer. That’s OK. And there are plenty of other reasons to keep a gathering small. Maybe the activity is something only some friends enjoy. Maybe two people don’t get along and you don’t want to spend your evening doing conflict resolution between martinis. Maybe you want to discuss something deeply personal with one or two people. Maybe you simply haven’t seen a particular friend in six months and want some one-on-one time.

Friendships are allowed to have subgroups. In fact, if you’ve known each other for more than about five minutes, they almost certainly do. However, there’s a big difference between saying “I need a smaller group right now” and “I want everyone to know they weren’t chosen.”

The case for inviting everyone

Hurt feelings. The hard part is that what feels like a perfectly reasonable invitation decision to one person can feel like a declaration of social leprosy to another. The person in the second or third circle may believe they’re in the inner circle—and they may find out they’re not because they open Instagram while eating Cap’n Crunch in bed. I know this because, well, see above.

Research suggests that social exclusion hurts in a very real way. A study from researchers at the University of Basel and Purdue University looked at the effects of ostracism in people’s everyday lives and found that these mundane experiences of being ignored or excluded can rock people’s fundamental feelings of safety, well-being and belonging. More recently, researchers from the University of Basel and the University of Koblenz-Landau looked specifically at social media exclusion. Across five studies involving 1,149 participants, they found that simply not being tagged in an Instagram post could torpedo people’s mental health, especially for those of us with a strong need to belong. Being cut out of a photo was even more upsetting. 

So yes, apparently our brains can look at a picture of six women eating nachos and react as though civilization itself has rejected us. That’s a pretty high emotional price for a plate of cheesy chips. Sometimes the message this sends is accidental, but sometimes it isn’t. Invitations are a way to exert power, control or status within a group. Even when the exclusion isn’t intentionally cruel, the message can still read: I chose them. I didn’t choose you.

Still, that doesn’t mean you should invite everyone to everything. It means that if you’re making a choice, you should understand the risks and recognize that it could have consequences for the friendship. 

The gray areas

I’m not sure I’ve ever covered an etiquette problem with so many gray areas. The whole answer is one giant gray area in a trench coat. Here are the questions I’d ask before deciding whether your guest list is perfectly reasonable or whether you’re about to become the villain in someone’s story arc.

How many people are being left out? If you have a group of 10 and you invite nine to the Friday-night hang, then you haven’t created an intimate situation—you’ve created a mean-girl group.

How often does this happen? If it’s just this once and you have a good reason, it’s probably not a big deal. But if the same person is mysteriously never invited—birthday party, Taco Tuesday, dancing naked under the full moon—then you need to consider if they are actually a friend.

How big is the original group? If you’re coordinating a girls’ night with 15 friends, then what is one more person? On the other hand, if you’re planning dinner for four, then yes, one or more people changes things significantly.

Is this actually a group? If these people are part of a clearly defined friend group that regularly does things together, excluding one or two people can feel much more pointed. But if you’re inviting a few mutuals who happen to be acquainted already, there may be no expectation that every social outing includes everyone.

How did the plan evolve? There’s a difference between “Two of us were already meeting up and two more people joined,” and “I made a list of 20 people and then selected the five people I like best.” The first feels organic. The second feels like The Bachelor, except nobody gets a rose and everyone gets screenshots.

Where is the night out happening? If you’re headed to a private spot or doing something that naturally limits the group size, you can be flexible. But if you are going to a very public place where you’ll run into mutuals or even possibly friends who weren’t invited, you should at least consider how that will feel. 

How official is the event? An official girls’ night out planned two weeks in advance with a calendar invite feels much different than a spontaneous trip to In-N-Out. Spontaneity gives you some etiquette grace.

Are kids or partners invited? Sometimes the friend group is just the girls, while other times it’s a family or couples event. Just make sure everyone knows which it is.

And most importantly: How will the person find out they weren’t invited? Ideally, they won’t. Realistically, they probably will. And if your friend has to find out about your dinner through an Instagram story, a tagged Facebook photo or a conversation at the gym, that can turn an otherwise reasonable decision into a much more painful one. 

What do you do about hurt feelings afterward?

My friend’s “just get over it” was rude, but at least she was honest. Too often, people try to hide or minimize the situation because they think they’re sparing the other person’s feelings. But once someone discovers that eight of their friends went out without them, their feelings are already hurt. Pretending otherwise doesn’t make the hurt disappear. It just adds a second layer of awkwardness.

You don’t necessarily need to apologize for having dinner with other people. You do need to acknowledge that your friend may feel bad. Something as simple as “I can understand why that hurt. It wasn’t meant to say anything about how I feel about you” can go a long way. Notice that I didn’t say “I’m sorry I went to dinner without you.” You are allowed to have other friends. You are allowed to have different friendships with different people. You are allowed to occasionally spend an evening with someone without forming a 30-person committee first.

What you are not allowed to do, if you want to remain a decent human being, is act baffled when someone feels excluded after discovering that the rest of the group went out without them. Feelings are not always logical. Unfortunately, they are also not optional.

The verdict

It is not rude to leave someone off the guest list. It can be rude to leave someone off the guest list. Yes, I realize that is an extremely unsatisfying answer. Welcome to etiquette.

You cannot invite everyone to everything, and you shouldn’t have to. Friendships naturally exist in different circles, and sometimes you want a quiet dinner with three people rather than a 30-person reunion that requires a seating chart and a project manager. articles.title: It’s Been 25 Years Since 9/11—These Are the 10 Most Powerful Stories About the Tragedy
articles.content:
Twenty-five years goes by in an instant. On Sept. 11, 2001, four planes were hijacked and pointed directly at the heart of the country, and life hasn’t been the same since. Though time can have a dulling effect, pushing those memories into a safe corner of one’s mind or lengthening the time between them, the awful visuals and lived experiences never go away.
It’s hard to believe, but a third of Americans were born after 9/11. But the effects of the attack—an enhanced surveillance state, increased airport security and military incursions around the world—are felt by everyone. Universal, too, are the stories of heroism, friendship and sacrifice that will forever mark that sad day.
With the 25th anniversary of 9/11 upon us, we put together a list of some of the most important journalism that took us through the day as it happened or examined it from the perspective of time. Ahead, we have 10 remarkable stories about Sept. 11, 2001. Some have been celebrated for decades; others you may never have read.
Read on to look back at the tragedy and perhaps find hope in some of the stories.

On Sept. 12, 2001, the Associated Press published a photograph of an unknown man falling headfirst from the north tower of the World Trade Center. The result explores collective grief and trauma and has become one of the defining pieces of journalism from the post–9/11 era.
Read more at Esquire
The title of this piece refers to the amount of time that elapsed between the first plane hitting the north tower at 8:46 a.m. and its collapse at 10:28 a.m. Eight months after the attack, the New York Times published an accounting of those 102 minutes by piecing together emails and phone calls from those trapped and killed, as well as recollections from survivors. It’s as chilling now as it was when it was first published.
Read more at The New York Times
The staff of the Wall Street Journal won the Pulitzer Prize for Breaking News Reporting in 2002 for its 9/11 coverage. That coverage included real-time reports of the planes and collapses as well as potential impacts, including to airport security and the economy, as they were happening. One particularly harrowing story is a first-person accounting of that day called “The Eye of the Storm: One Journey Through Desperation and Chaos,” by John Bussey.
You can read all of the winning coverage at the Pulitzer Prize page, below.
Read more at The Pulitzer Prizes
This narrative account, published just days after 9/11, weaves together events at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and the final moments of United Flight 93, which went down in Pennsylvania. David Maraniss reconstructs the day through survivor accounts and reporting that paint a vivid picture of the chaos and destruction, as well as how it was seen through the eyes of people living through it in real time.
Read more at The Washington Post
Jennifer Senior’s devastating account of one family’s loss after the attacks won the 2022 Pulitzer Prize for Feature Writing. Bobby McIlvaine was just 26 years old on Sept. 11, 2001, and the story of the different ways his family coped with losing their charming and ambitious son, brother and boyfriend reminds us that grief is unpredictable and personal.
Read more at The Atlantic
Rick Resorla, a former British paratrooper and U.S. Army veteran, was the head of security for Morgan Stanley in the south tower of the World Trade Center. Credited with saving thousands of people, he died when he went back inside to offer more help. This piece by James B. Stewart tells the story of that day through the lens of Resorla’s personal life before the attacks, as well as through his loved ones, who subsequently had to process his heroism and death.
Read more at The New Yorker
This story, published just weeks after 9/11, looks at the lives of five people who were affected by the attacks and how they dealt with the immediate aftermath. A priest delivers a mass, a widow gives her daughter a bath, a firefighter can’t stop thinking of falling bodies. It’s an intimate look at “five people out of the multitudes,” and it stays with you.
Read more at The Washington Post

This story, which won a James Beard Award for Best Personal Essay, is told by Cal Sussman, a writer who took a wine class and then became a sommelier at Windows on the World. It works through survivor’s grief and paints a touching portrait of a beloved New York City institution.
Read more at Esquire
Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark worked on the south tower’s 81st and 84th floors, respectively, and they are two of only four known survivors of the floors above the impact zone. Clark made the fateful decision to go down the only open stairwell, ignoring pleas from others to go up to the roof, and heard Praimnath calling for help. Both reached the ground floor and ran from the building just as it collapsed, and they are still friends to this day.
Read more at The Guardian
This comprehensive retrospective of the first minutes of the attack combines narrative text, photography, video and data journalism to tell the story of what was happening on the ground as the day unfolded. The 17 minutes refers to the time between the first plane hitting the north tower and the second hitting the south one, and reporter Garrett M. Graff highlights a range of accounts from regular people as well as military and government officials about the confusion of that day.
Read more at National Geographic

articles.title: You’ll Never Guess How the Football Huddle Got Its Start—Here’s the Fascinating History Behind This Strategy
articles.content:
I firmly believe that the only good thing about the end of summer is the beginning of football season. Though I’m a die-hard New York Giants fan (it’s been a rough few years, but things are gonna turn around!), I’ll watch any and every game I can. On Sundays—and Monday and Thursday nights—from Week 1 through the postseason, you’ll find me near a TV, very likely yelling at the announcers.
But even if the extent of your football knowledge is the name of the team your family roots for, you’ve seen the huddle: The action ends, the players wander back toward one another, and suddenly they’re standing shoulder to shoulder in a little circle. There’s some serious discussion, a few nods, and then they break apart and race to their positions.
It happens over and over, in every football game. It’s such a familiar part of the sport that most of us never stop to wonder about it. But why do football players huddle?
As it turns out, this football staple has a very distinct origin—and it’s one you’d likely never guess. For the deets on one of football’s most recognizable rituals, I turned to two experts: football historian Ken Crippen, founder of the Football Learning Academy, and Jon Kendle, vice president of Archives and Exhibits at the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
Whether you know a blitz from a nickel package or just enjoy the game (or the snacks), we guarantee that you’ll find this fascinating. Read on for the answer before kickoff.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, entertainment, humor, travel and tech.
The roots of American football trace back to both soccer and rugby, with the first college football game between Rutgers and Princeton in 1869. In the 1880s, Yale player and coach Walter Camp, who became known as the “father of American football,” helped establish rules that increasingly separated American football from rugby.
The game was barely recognizable by today’s standards. “When it first emerged, forward passing was illegal,” says Crippen. “You would see mass-momentum plays and a lot of physicality.”
And that physicality could be deadly. “So many players died on the field that they would have running counts in the newspapers,” he adds. Football was a game still figuring itself out, from how it was played to how teams communicated in the middle of it.
In the early days of football, quarterbacks simply called or signaled the play—often right at the line of scrimmage. Of course, this “was a problem because the defense could hear the play call,” Crippen notes.
Another option was to call the play while the team was approaching the line of scrimmage, “but far enough away that the defense could not hear them,” he says.
That created an obvious strategic problem: If the defense could hear the play call, it could adjust accordingly. Teams needed a way to communicate without giving away their plans.
The football huddle is widely credited to Gallaudet College, now Gallaudet University, a school for deaf students in Washington, D.C. Gallaudet’s football team was made up of deaf players who communicated using sign language, creating a unique challenge on the field.
Because their opponents were often schools for the hearing-impaired, Gallaudet quarterback Paul Hubbard worried they were watching his hands to read his team’s intentions, according to Kendle. Hubbard’s solution was to form a circle so opponents couldn’t read his signs.
That circle became the first football huddle. The exact game in which it debuted is unknown, but Crippen says the practice appears to have developed organically during Gallaudet’s 1894 season, when the team primarily played the Pennsylvania School for the Deaf and the New York School for the Deaf.
The huddle—which Kendle calls “a magical and special place of trust”—didn’t immediately become a universal part of football.
Amos Alonzo Stagg, one of the sport’s great early innovators, began using the huddle while coaching at the University of Chicago in 1896. But it took a while for the rest of football to catch on. “Stagg was an innovator, and whatever he did was usually copied by other college teams,” Crippen says. Still, the huddle “did not really catch on until the 1920s.”
But the huddle’s usefulness created a new problem: Teams could use it to waste time. “Some saw it as an intentional stall tactic,” Crippen says. That led to rules in the 1930s designed to keep teams from spending too much time in the huddle. Eventually, the introduction of the play clock in 1976 made those restrictions unnecessary. Today, the NFL gives offenses a set amount of time to begin the next play.
Here’s the funny thing: There’s no rule saying a football team needs to huddle. According to the current NFL Rulebook, “a huddle is the action of two or more players in the field of play or in the end zone who, instead of assuming their normal position for the snap, free kick or fair catch kick, form a group for receiving instructions for the next play or for any other reason.”
What happens inside that circle is up to the offense. In a typical huddle, the quarterback communicates instructions for the next play. That, notes Kendle, can “be for the formation, motions, snap count, blocking schemes, wide receiver routes and which gap the running back should run through.”
The huddle also gives the offense a moment to take stock. “It allows the team to see who is hurt, tired or seeing something that the offense can take advantage of against the defense,” Crippen says.
Kendle adds that the huddle can conceal the offense’s formation, making it more difficult for the defense to line up correctly before the snap.
Because sometimes the best way to beat a defense is to deny it time to respond. Enter the no-huddle offense: Rather than gathering to discuss the next play, the offense lines up immediately. The NFL describes it as a strategy that can conserve time, catch the defense off guard and prevent defensive substitutions.
In the 1980s and early 1990s, the Cincinnati Bengals and Buffalo Bills featured “no-huddle” offenses, according to Kendle. The Bills and their “hurry-up” offense advanced to four consecutive Super Bowls.
By the way: No-huddle football is hardly new. Crippen traces its use back to John Heisman (yes, the trophy is named for him), who used the offense at Auburn in 1899.
If the huddle was invented to make communication easier and more secretive, modern technology has made communicating plays much easier.
In the 1940s, Cleveland Browns coach Paul Brown used a “messenger guard” system, in which a substitute player could enter the game with the play from the sideline. Brown also experimented with radio headsets in the 1950s, though it wasn’t until 1994 that the NFL instituted radio helmets to allow limited communication from the sidelines to the quarterback on the field, according to Kendle.
Technology has continued to advance football communication. In 2023, Gallaudet University and AT&T debuted a 5G-connected football helmet that allowed a coach to select a play on a tablet and send it to a digital display inside the quarterback’s helmet.
Probably not—or, at least, not entirely.
“I believe the huddle is still an essential part of football,” Kendle says. “It allows the team to come together as a unit to receive critical instructions and make sure they are on the same page.”
So the next time you watch a football game and see the offense gather around their quarterback, take a second to appreciate what you’re actually looking at. The huddle may look like a simple pause between plays, but it’s one of football’s most enduring strategic tools—giving players a moment to communicate, regroup and figure out what comes next.
Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have a football game to watch.
